summaries.summary: This slice contains the front matter, preface, and a run of dated blog-post chapters that move from Vim basics and writing workflows to Neovim, sessions, JavaScript tooling, git, a minimal .vimrc, and file-navigation alternatives, ending with the author's closing essay. It is a practical, opinionated collection of tips rather than a systematic Vim manual.

This slice contains the cookbook's front matter (title page and a 236-entry table of contents) and the full recipe body: the “First things” introduction plus 21 chapters of 209 short Problem/Solution recipes, from navigation and search through substitution, global commands, macros and registers, tags, text generation, terminal usage, visual mode, and vimrc/window configuration. Examples are command-focused and assume the reader types along.

This slice covers the front matter and Part I through most of Chapter 6: vi/Vim basics, cursor movement, simple editing, the ex line editor, and global replacement with regular expressions. It is largely tutorial prose interspersed with keystroke demos, command tables, exercises, and cross-references.

This slice finishes Chapter 6's treatment of global replacement (POSIX bracket expressions, replacement metacharacters, and pattern-matching examples) and works through Chapter 7's advanced editing material: :set and .exrc configuration, Unix command filters, abbreviations, maps, @-functions, ex scripts, ctags, and indentation control. It then opens Part II with Chapter 8's overview of Vim's history and features (startup files, motions, visual mode, extended regular expressions, undo, incremental search) and Chapter 9's first half on gvim menus, toolbars, and running gvim under WSL.

This slice moves from gvim GUI options under WSL/X Windows into Vim’s multiwindow and buffer model, then surveys programmer features such as folding, indenting, completion, tags, syntax highlighting, and QuickFix. It closes with Vim scripting and autocommands, followed by Chapter 13’s tour of spellchecking, binary editing, digraphs, remote file editing, directory browsing, and backups.

This slice finishes Chapter 13’s survey of Vim enhancements (HTML conversion, vimdiff, viminfo and :mksession, long-line display, abbreviations, and quick tricks) and works through Chapter 14’s power techniques: convenience mappings, the command-line and search-history windows, awk-based buffer filtering and word-frequency analysis, and an enhanced status line. It then covers Vim as an IDE (plug-in managers, NERDTree, Fugitive, completion, Termdebug), vi’s presence in shells, screen, browsers, Word, and other tools, the epilogue, and the opening of Appendix A’s vi/ex command reference.

This slice completes Appendix A's alphabetical ex command reference, then presents Appendix B's set-option tables for “Heirloom”/Solaris vi and Vim 8.2, Appendix C's vi miscellany (project files, logos, the Vim clutch, Towers of Hanoi macros, the vi-versus-Emacs debate, quotations), and Appendix D's guidance on obtaining and building vi and Vim on Unix, Windows, and macOS. It ends where the book's alphabetical Index begins.

Summary: this slice contains no instructional prose. It is the tail of the book's alphabetical back-of-book index (headwords from 'bottom-line command overview' through 'ZZ to quit and save', covering letters S-Z), followed by two back-matter sections, 'About the Authors' (biographies of Arnold Robbins and Elbert Hannah) and the 'Colophon' describing the tarsier cover animal.

This slice covers the front matter, introduction, and Chapters 1-6 plus the opening of Chapter 7 (Tips 1-28, ending inside Tip 28): installing Vim 8 and Neovim, Vim packages and minpac, fuzzy/semantic file opening with fzf and Projectionist, the quickfix list with Dispatch, ALE, Grepper and vim-test, Neovim's terminal emulator, sessions and persistent undo, and context-sensitive configuration with autocommands and EditorConfig.

This slice finishes the chapter on configuring Vim per project: ALE linters and ‘textwidth’ are driven from .projections.json metadata via Projectionist queries and a User ProjectionistActivate autocommand, with notes on projection specificity, generic keys, local vimrc risks, and built-in projection keys. It then opens Appendix 1, which surveys future directions for Vim 8 and Neovim (LSP, :terminal, externalized tab bar/pop-up menu/status line GUIs, and embedding Neovim in Sublime Text and VSCode), and closes with footnotes, the bibliography, and back matter.

PDF-derived clean text of Alvaro Leal's Neovim guide: installation and basic editing commands, Lua configuration (options, keymaps, functions, Packer), plugin setup for colorschemes, LSP, Telescope, gitsigns and nvim-dap, and a closing tour of Vim movements. The page blocks are out of book order (figures 19-46 precede figures 1-18) and stray page markers plus a collapsed command table survive in the flow.

This slice covers the front matter (publisher notes, Read Me, notation conventions) and Parts 1-4 through the opening of Chapter 10: the Vim way and the dot command, Normal/Insert/Visual/Command-Line modes, buffers and files, motions and jumps, and the start of the registers chapter. It is instructional prose organized as 60 numbered tips, dense with keystroke/buffer tables and cross-references.

This slice begins inside Chapter 10 (registers and the system clipboard), covers Chapters 11-21 (macros, matching patterns and literals, search, substitution, global commands, ctags, the quickfix list, project-wide grep/vimgrep, autocompletion, and spell checking), and ends with Appendix 1's vimrc primer. It is organized as Tips 61-123 with keystroke/buffer tables, code excerpts, and cross-references.

This slice covers Pro Vim's front matter, Introduction, Chapters 1-10, and the opening of Chapter 11: terminal/Vim setup, Vim fundamentals (commands, buffers, windows, tabs, modes), files, editing commands, registers, folding, VISUAL-BLOCK mode, bulk command processing, and editing workflow. It is mostly tutorial prose with shell/VimL configuration listings, command tables, and worked examples, and it ends as Chapter 11 starts its search-and-replace material.

This slice runs from the end of Pro Vim's search-and-replace chapter through chapters on buffers/windows/tabs, automation and macros, change and jump lists, marks, sessions, plug-ins, diffing, custom commands, terminal integration, working with code, practical tips, and the opening of the tmux section. It is broadly usable for curriculum mapping, but the marks chapter (roughly lines 7595-7815) is badly corrupted and several promised directory trees/diagrams are absent.

This slice closes Pro Vim's tmux section (Chapters 24-30): it covers tmux sessions, buffers and copy mode, panes and windows, customization via shell wrappers and key bindings, copy/paste and clipboard workarounds, scripting with send-keys and tmuxinator, pair programming via tmate and Vagrant, and the workflow tools Reptyr and tmux-resurrect. The final ~400 lines are the book's back index.

Summary: this opening slice runs from the Leanpub front matter through the first three major sections of the tutorial, arguing why Vim is worth learning and then teaching modality, the count–operator–motion command pattern, movement, undo/redo, .vimrc settings, registers, visual marking, insert-mode completion, macros, mappings, colors, quickfix, tags, marks, and alternate-file navigation. It ends with the Epilog's short list of habits.

This slice is the complete Vim 101 Hacks text: front matter, 15 chapters, 101 numbered hacks, and 15 bonus hacks covering Vim basics, navigation, text manipulation, programmer features, command-line and gVim options, search, completion, and folding. Each hack is a short, example-driven recipe built from normal-mode commands, ex commands, and .vimrc settings.

This slice is a cheatsheet-style Vim reference covering the four main modes, motion and editing commands, text objects, registers, search and replace with Vim regular expressions, macros, vimrc customization, and command-line startup options.
